question: Can several examiner models, or a trained examiner, make cross-examination better at detecting factual errors?
asked_by: Cohen et al., LM vs LM: Detecting Factual Errors via Cross Examination
remaining_question: Does training the examiner's question generation (e.g. with RL rewarded on detection correctness), or pooling several diverse examiners, raise cross-examination F1 at detecting factual errors above a single prompted examiner with a majority-vote or trained (e.g. linear) decision rule, and do correlated mistakes across capable examiner LMs limit the gain from pooling?

blockers.name: A measurement
blockers.next: Train the examiner's question generation (for example with RL rewarded on detection correctness) or pool diverse examiners, compare cross-examination F1 with a single prompted examiner using a majority-vote or trained decision rule, and measure correlated mistakes across examiners.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2501.01558v4: Predicting the Performance of Black-box LLMs through Follow-up Queries
findings.claim: The authors ask a black-box model follow-up questions, take the probabilities of its responses as representations, and train a linear model on them that, they report, reliably and accurately predicts model correctness on question-answering and reasoning benchmarks and can even outperform white-box linear predictors that operate over model internals or activations. Predictive performance increased as the number of elicitation prompts increased, with the rate of increase slowly diminishing. The questions are fixed prompts treated as abstract features; the authors note that further work could perform discrete optimization over the prompts.
findings.setting: Experiment: black-box LLMs as examined models; question-answering and reasoning benchmarks; fixed follow-up questions; trained linear predictors on response probabilities predicting answer correctness. Not an interactive cross-examination of a claim, and no examiner model is trained.
findings.bears_on: Both parts, partially: a trained decision rule over many follow-up questions detects incorrect answers and more questions help; training the question-generating examiner, and using several examiner models, are not tested.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2309.15840v1: How to Catch an AI Liar: Lie Detection in Black-Box LLMs by Asking Unrelated Questions
findings.claim: A logistic-regression classifier on a model's yes/no answers to a predefined set of unrelated follow-up questions detected lies with high accuracy and, when trained only on GPT-3.5 prompted to lie about factual questions, generalised to other LLM architectures, LLMs fine-tuned to lie, sycophantic lies and lies emerging in real-life scenarios such as sales. The authors did not choose the elicitation questions systematically and list detectors using inconsistency checks or iterative interrogation as future work.
findings.setting: Experiment: black-box lie detection; GPT-3.5 training setting, transfer to other LLMs and lie types; fixed elicitation questions, trained logistic regression. Lies are defined as false statements the model 'knows' are false, not honest factual errors.
findings.bears_on: Trained-examiner part, by analogy: training the decision rule of a follow-up-question detector works for lies; the questions themselves were not trained.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2311.01740v2: SAC3: Reliable Hallucination Detection in Black-Box Language Models via Semantic-aware Cross-check Consistency
findings.claim: In a scenario where the dataset only contains hallucinated samples (accuracy of detecting hallucinated samples at a preset threshold of 0.5), the model-level cross-check with verifier LMs performed well on the prime-number dataset but failed to accurately detect hallucination on the senator-search dataset, because both verifier LMs refused to answer a large portion of its questions for lack of sufficient information. By combining the target LM, SAC3-all with Guanaco-33b achieved the highest detection accuracy compared with SC2 (+51.2%), SAC3-Q (+6.2%) and SAC3-QM (+5.0%).
findings.setting: Experiment: hallucination detection by self-checking (SC2) and cross-check variants (SAC3-Q, SAC3-QM, SAC3-all); target LM gpt-3.5-turbo; verifier LM Falcon-7b-instruct or Guanaco-33b; prime-number and senator-search datasets, in the scenario where the dataset contains only hallucinated samples, with a preset threshold of 0.5. The verifier LMs are asked the questions themselves; there is no examiner dialogue or cross-examination of the target LM.
findings.bears_on: Several-examiner part, by analogy: adding another model's answers helps only where that model has the relevant knowledge.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2603.24579v1: MARCH: Multi-Agent Reinforced Self-Check for LLM Hallucination
findings.claim: MARCH has three agents: a Solver generates an initial RAG response, a Proposer decomposes it into claim-level verifiable atomic propositions, and a Checker validates these propositions against retrieved evidence in isolation, without the Solver's original output. For each question generated by the Proposer, the Checker generates multiple independent audit trajectories and a majority vote determines the consensus answer. The shared policy of the three agents is optimised with PPO (multi-agent RL). From Llama3.1-8B, the policy trained on General QA data improved the average accuracy from 29.7 to 51.6 (+21.9) and the policy trained on STEM data reached 52.3 (+22.6), with gains across all eight dimensions; the authors say these 8B policies reach or surpass the performance of many much larger judge models.
findings.setting: Experiment: retrieval-augmented generation; one shared policy for Solver, Proposer and Checker, starting from Llama3.1-8B and trained with multi-agent RL (PPO) on General QA or STEM data; evaluated on hallucination benchmarks and on average accuracy over eight dimensions, compared with judge models. The Checker verifies against retrieved evidence, not by cross-examining the examinee's other beliefs, and the questions come from the system's own Proposer.
findings.bears_on: Trained-examiner part, by analogy: training a question-proposing verification pipeline improved its factual-consistency judgments in a RAG setting.
